questionText: Listen to a conversation in the student center where a student reflects on a recent summer internship with a career advisor.
audioScript:
Situation: A student stops by the career services desk in the student center to reflect on a recently completed summer internship and discuss next steps.
Career Advisor: Hi Tyler, welcome back. How did your summer internship at the environmental consulting firm go?
Tyler: It was great, honestly better than I expected. I spent the first two weeks mostly shadowing senior analysts, but by week three they let me run my own small site assessment for a wetland restoration project.
Career Advisor: That's impressive. Were you working independently or as part of a team?
Tyler: I had a mentor, a senior analyst named Karen, who reviewed all my work. But I was responsible for collecting soil samples, writing the field report, and presenting findings to the project manager. That presentation was nerve-wracking.
Career Advisor: I can imagine. What was the most valuable thing you took away from the experience?
Tyler: I'd say learning how to communicate technical findings to non-technical clients. In class, we write for professors who already know the science. But the client at the restoration project was a city planner who just wanted to know if the wetland was recovering. I had to translate jargon into plain language.
Career Advisor: That's a crucial professional skill. Did the firm offer you a return offer for next summer?
Tyler: They did, actually. Karen said they'd love to have me back, and there's a possibility of a part-time remote role during the semester if I'm interested. I'm leaning toward it, but I want to make sure it won't interfere with my thesis.
Career Advisor: A good rule of thumb is to cap outside work at ten hours per week during your final year. I'd also recommend updating your resume and LinkedIn now while the experience is fresh, and asking Karen for a recommendation letter before she gets too busy.
Tyler: That's smart. I'll email her this week. Thanks for the advice.

questionText: Listen to a conversation in the academic office where a student gets feedback on an upcoming research presentation.
audioScript:
Situation: A graduate student visits her professor's office to get feedback on an upcoming research presentation for a campus symposium.
Professor Diaz: Come in, Nina. I reviewed the draft slides you sent last night. You've made good progress since the outline stage.
Nina: Thank you, Professor Diaz. I'm a bit nervous because this will be my first time presenting at the graduate research symposium. The audience will include faculty from other departments.
Professor Diaz: That's understandable. Let's start with the structure. Your introduction is solid, but you spend six slides on background literature. For a fifteen-minute talk, trim it to two slides. The audience needs just enough context to understand your research question.
Nina: Okay, I can condense it. My main concern is the methodology section. I used a mixed-methods approach, combining surveys with follow-up interviews. Is that too much to cover in the time allotted?
Professor Diaz: It's ambitious, but manageable if you're selective. Present the survey results as a summary chart, not individual data points. Then highlight two interview quotes that illustrate your key finding. Don't try to report every theme.
Nina: That makes sense. What about the results section? I have three main findings, but I'm not sure which one to emphasize.
Professor Diaz: Lead with the finding about how peer feedback improves writing confidence. That's the most novel contribution and directly answers your research question. The other two findings can be mentioned briefly as secondary results.
Nina: Should I include a limitations slide? My committee chair said it shows scholarly maturity.
Professor Diaz: Absolutely, one slide at the end. Acknowledge the small sample size and the fact that your participants were all from one university. Then suggest future research with a larger, more diverse sample.
Nina: Got it. Last question, how should I handle the Q&A? I'm worried about questions I can't answer.
Professor Diaz: That's normal. If you don't know an answer, acknowledge it honestly and explain how you might investigate it. Never make up data. Practice your talk at least three times aloud, and time yourself. I'd also suggest doing a dry run with your lab mates this Thursday.

questionText: Listen to a conversation on campus about a student attending a campus budget hearing.
audioScript:
Situation: A student representative discusses the upcoming campus budget hearing with the student government treasurer to prepare testimony about library funding.
Treasurer Marcus: Hey Elena, thanks for coming. The campus budget hearing is next Wednesday at six PM in the main lecture hall. Are you still planning to speak on behalf of the library expansion proposal?
Elena: Yes, I am. I've never testified at a budget hearing before, though. Can you walk me through how it works?
Treasurer Marcus: Sure. Each speaker gets three minutes at the podium. You'll sign in at the door and they'll call names in order. The panel includes the vice chancellor for finance, three deans, and two student government representatives.
Elena: Three minutes is really short. What should I prioritize?
Treasurer Marcus: Lead with a personal story. Last semester, you couldn't find study space during finals week, right? Use that to show the human impact. Then state the specific ask: the library needs funding to add a twenty-four-hour study wing with forty additional seats.
Elena: That's a good angle. Do I need to bring data too?
Treasurer Marcus: Definitely. The library director compiled a report showing that seat occupancy hit ninety-two percent during peak hours last fall. Bring a one-page handout with that statistic and the projected cost. The estimate is one hundred twenty thousand dollars for renovation.
Elena: One hundred twenty thousand sounds like a lot. Won't the panel push back on the price tag?
Treasurer Marcus: They might. Be ready to mention that the Student Activities Council endorsed the proposal unanimously, and that a petition gathered over eight hundred student signatures. Numbers like that show broad support.
Elena: Good point. What happens after the hearing?
Treasurer Marcus: The panel reviews all testimony and submits a funding recommendation to the chancellor within two weeks. The chancellor makes the final decision, which is usually announced in March. I'll forward you the budget guidelines document so you can reference the exact funding line item.
Elena: Perfect. I'll draft my remarks tonight and send them to you for review.
Treasurer Marcus: Sounds great. Just remember, speak clearly and don't rush. Three minutes is enough if you're concise.

questionText: Listen to a conversation in the student center about organizing a table at the student club fair.
audioScript:
Situation: Two students and a student activities coordinator discuss how to set up an engaging table for their new robotics club at the upcoming student club fair.
Coordinator: Hi guys, thanks for stopping by. You're registering the Robotics Club for the student club fair on September twelfth, correct?
Jordan: Yes, that's right. This is our first year as an official club, so we want to make a strong impression and recruit at least thirty new members.
Coordinator: Great goal. Let me walk you through the logistics. The fair runs from ten AM to three PM on the main quad. Each club gets one table, two chairs, and a tablecloth in the university colors.
Priya: What about electricity? We'd love to run a demo of our small robot picking up objects.
Coordinator: You can request electricity, but there are only eight powered spots on the quad. I see four are still available, so I'll reserve one for you. Just bring your own extension cord, at least twenty-five feet.
Jordan: Perfect. Are there any restrictions on what we can display?
Coordinator: No open flames, no helium balloons because of the ceiling in the backup indoor location, and all demonstrations must stay within your table footprint so walkways stay clear.
Priya: Understood. Our robot stays on the table, so that should be fine. Do we need to bring our own sign-up sheet?
Coordinator: I'd recommend using the digital sign-up QR code instead. The student activities office generates one for each club. Students scan it with their phones and their info goes straight to a spreadsheet. It's much more reliable than paper.
Jordan: That's convenient. Is there a way to get on the campus map or brochure?
Coordinator: Yes, clubs registered by today are automatically listed in the fair brochure with a one-line description. I already have your description: 'Robotics Club: building and programming autonomous robots for competitions.' Does that work?
Priya: That's exactly what we wanted. One more question, can we give out candy to attract students?
Coordinator: Individually wrapped candy is fine. Just no homemade food items. Now, I should mention there's a mandatory orientation for all club table hosts this Friday at four PM in room two-oh-one. It covers safety guidelines and fair day procedures.

questionText: Listen to a conversation in the academic office about a student planning for graduation requirements.
audioScript:
Situation: A senior student meets with the registrar to verify graduation requirements, resolve a missing grade, and confirm the commencement ceremony details.
Registrar: Good afternoon, Devon. I've pulled up your graduation audit. You're on track to graduate this May, but there are two items we need to resolve.
Devon: Hi, thanks for seeing me. What are the two issues?
Registrar: First, your capstone course, History 490, shows an incomplete grade from last semester. Professor Whitfield submitted a grade change form, but it hasn't been processed yet. Second, you're missing the upper-division writing requirement.
Devon: The incomplete is because I had a medical extension. I submitted my final paper two weeks ago and Professor Whitfield said she'd file the change. For the writing requirement, I thought my history seminar counted.
Registrar: History 475 does count, but only if you took the writing-intensive section. You registered for the standard section, which doesn't carry that designation. You'd need either to petition to have your work in that course evaluated, or take a one-credit writing portfolio workshop this semester.
Devon: The workshop sounds faster. When does it meet?
Registrar: It meets every other Friday from two to four PM, starting next week. You'd compile three writing samples from your upper-division courses and submit a reflective essay. The deadline to register for the workshop is this Friday.
Devon: I'll sign up today. Now, about commencement, I wanted to confirm the ceremony date and cap-and-gown ordering.
Registrar: Commencement is Saturday, May eighteenth, at ten AM in the stadium. If it rains, they move it to the field house, but that's been announced in advance only twice in twenty years. You need to order your cap and gown through the bookstore's online portal by April first. After that, there's a late fee of twenty-five dollars.
Devon: What about tickets for my family? My parents and two siblings want to come.
Registrar: Each graduate gets four guest tickets. You can request up to two additional tickets through a lottery system, but those aren't guaranteed. The lottery opens March fifteenth and closes March twenty-second.
Devon: Four tickets should be enough, but I'll enter the lottery just in case. Is there a graduation rehearsal?
Registrar: Yes, rehearsal is mandatory and takes place the Friday before commencement at two PM. You'll receive your name card and learn the procession order. Don't miss it, because your diploma won't be at commencement if you skip rehearsal.

questionText: Listen to a conversation in the academic office about a student making the most of faculty office hours.
audioScript:
Situation: A first-year student visits her academic advisor to discuss how to effectively use faculty office hours after struggling to connect with a professor.
Advisor Kim: Have a seat, Sofia. You mentioned in your email that you're having trouble approaching Professor Reynolds for help in your economics course. Tell me more.
Sofia: Thanks, Advisor Kim. I'm enrolled in Econ 102, and I'm finding the problem sets really difficult. I went to Professor Reynolds's office hours twice, but both times there were five or six other students waiting. By the time it was my turn, I felt rushed and couldn't fully explain what I didn't understand.
Advisor Kim: That's a common frustration in large introductory courses. A few strategies can help. First, have you checked whether Professor Reynolds holds office hours on different days? Some professors offer both morning and afternoon slots, and the afternoon sessions tend to be less crowded.
Sofia: I only went on Tuesday mornings. Let me check the syllabus. Yes, he also has Thursdays from three to four thirty PM.
Advisor Kim: Try that slot. Second, come prepared with specific questions. Instead of saying 'I don't get chapter four,' point to a particular problem and explain exactly where your reasoning breaks down. Professors appreciate targeted questions because they can help efficiently.
Sofia: That makes sense. I usually just say I'm confused generally. I'll write down my steps before I go.
Advisor Kim: Good. Third, if the regular office hours don't work, you can always email to request a separate appointment. Keep the email concise: state the course, the topic you need help with, and propose two or three time windows. Professors are more likely to respond to a well-structured request.
Sofia: Should I mention that I've already attempted the problems? I don't want to seem like I'm asking for answers.
Advisor Kim: Exactly. Show your work. That signals you're putting in effort, not looking for a shortcut. Also, consider forming a study group and bringing a shared question. Sometimes a group visit is more productive and less intimidating.
Sofia: There's a study group that meets Wednesdays. I could bring a question from there. One more thing, does it look bad if I attend office hours every week?
Advisor Kim: Not at all. Consistent attendance shows engagement. Just be respectful of other students' time. If you've resolved your main issue, step aside and let others have a turn. You can also use the economics tutoring center for routine practice, saving office hours for the genuinely difficult conceptual questions.

To convince Sofia to switch her major
To report Professor Reynolds for poor teaching
To plan Sofia's schedule for next semester
questions.explanation: Advisor Kim provides Sofia with multiple strategies, from timing to question preparation to email etiquette, to help her use office hours effectively.
